role: Veterans Law Judge of the Board of Veterans' Appeals writing a decision on a veteran's appeal from a Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Regional Office disability decision, articulating Title 38 service-connection / increased-rating / TDIU / CUE doctrine, weighing service treatment records, VA examinations, private medical opinions and lay statements under the benefit-of-the-doubt rule
target: a veteran's claim for service connection, increased rating, TDIU, earlier effective date, CUE, or other VA benefit, as evidenced by service treatment records, VA examinations, private medical opinions, lay statements, and procedural posture under the Appeals Modernization Act or legacy review system
inline_evidence_example: the phrase "The Board finds the September 2023 private psychiatric evaluation report and accompanying opinion of low probative value. While Dr. Q.A. provides an opinion that the Veteran's depressive disorder began during active service, Dr. Q.A. does not provide a rationale or reconcile the negative evidence of record. See Nieves-Rodriguez v. Peake, 22 Vet. App. 295 (2008); Stefl v. Nicholson, 21 Vet. App. 120, 124 (2007)" is a complaint that evidences a 'medical-opinion-adequacy / Nieves-Rodriguez probative-weight' norm; the phrase "As there is no contrary medical evidence of record, the Board concludes that service connection for erectile dysfunction, as secondary to the Veteran's service-connected emphysema with COPD, is warranted" is an observation that evidences a 'secondary-service-connection under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310 — uncontested-nexus' norm; the phrase "the Veteran is competent to report having experienced pain in service and the 1972 separation examination notes corroborate his statements, establishing in-service incurrence under Layno" is an observation that evidences a 'lay-evidence competency and corroboration under Layno v. Brown' norm; the phrase "Affording the Veteran the benefit of the doubt, the Veteran was unemployable beginning August 2018 to prior to October 9, 2019, due to his service-connected disabilities" is an observation that evidences a 'benefit-of-the-doubt under 38 U.S.C. § 5107(b)' norm applied to TDIU; the phrase "As the rating criteria are indistinguishable, it provides the Veteran no greater benefit to be rated under Diagnostic Code 6603 as opposed to Diagnostic Code 6604, or vice versa. ... separate ratings ... would constitute pyramiding" is an observation that evidences a 'pyramiding prohibition under 38 C.F.R. § 4.14' norm; the phrase "Dr. R.T.'s conclusory statement that the Veteran's left knee should be rated as 50 to 75 percent disabling is deemed to be of no probative value" is a complaint that evidences a 'medical-opinion must be supported by rationale, not conclusory' norm.
polarity_hint:
BVA decisions are written in the Board's formal, third-person, declarative voice and are dominated by EVIDENCE-WEIGHING and DOCTRINAL-APPLICATION moves rather than overt complaint or praise of the veteran. Common norms surfaced: (i) the three Caluza/Shedden/Hickson elements of service connection (current disability, in-service event/injury/disease, nexus); (ii) presumptive service connection for chronic diseases under 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.307, 3.309(a), Walker v. Shinseki for non-chronic-listed conditions; (iii) presumptive Agent Orange / herbicide exposure (38 C.F.R. § 3.309(e), Procopio v. Wilkie for blue-water Navy, Combee v. Brown for non-presumptive theory); (iv) Gulf War undiagnosed illness under 38 C.F.R. § 3.317; (v) secondary service connection under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310 (Allen v. Brown for aggravation); (vi) probative weight of medical opinions under Nieves-Rodriguez v. Peake (rationale, file review, accuracy of reported history) and Stefl v. Nicholson; (vii) competence-vs-credibility of lay evidence under Layno v. Brown, Jandreau v. Nicholson, Buchanan v. Nicholson; (viii) benefit-of-the-doubt rule under 38 U.S.C. § 5107(b), Lynch v. McDonough (equipoise); (ix) increased-rating analysis under specific Diagnostic Codes (38 C.F.R. § 4.71a musculoskeletal, § 4.85/4.86 hearing, § 4.97 respiratory, § 4.130 mental); (x) functional-loss / DeLuca / Mitchell / Correia / Sharp considerations for musculoskeletal flares and ROM testing; (xi) staged ratings (Fenderson, Hart); (xii) pyramiding prohibition (38 C.F.R. § 4.14); (xiii) TDIU under 38 C.F.R. § 4.16 with schedular threshold and substantially-gainful-occupation analysis (Hatlestad, Van Hoose); (xiv) CUE: outcome-determinative error, manifestly different result (38 C.F.R. § 3.105, Russell v. Principi, Fugo v. Brown); (xv) effective-date rules (38 U.S.C. § 5110, 38 C.F.R. § 3.400); (xvi) AMA-docket evidence-window constraints (38 C.F.R. § 20.300, 20.302, 20.303). Praise and complaint are almost always directed at EVIDENCE OR REASONING the Board is weighing — not at the veteran. Specifically: (i) the Board PRAISES a medical opinion or examination when it satisfies Nieves-Rodriguez ("the VA examiner conducted a thorough review of the claims file and provided a detailed rationale"); (ii) the Board COMPLAINS about a medical opinion when it is conclusory, lacks rationale, misstates the veteran's history, or fails to reconcile negative evidence; (iii) the Board makes OBSERVATIONS when stating the governing doctrine, applying a Diagnostic Code threshold, finding lay evidence competent or credible, or concluding the evidence is in equipoise; (iv) the Board uses SUGGESTION when instructing the AOJ on remand ("the AOJ should obtain an addendum opinion that addresses ...") or when stating a prescriptive doctrinal rule ("to establish service connection, there must be evidence of ..."). signal_type ENUM IS STRICTLY {complaint, praise, observation, suggestion}. Most signals will be `observation` with polarity `neutral` (doctrinal exposition) or `praise`/`complaint` of medical evidence with polarity `positive`/`negative`. 

DATASET-SPECIFIC OVERRIDES (these REPLACE the generic constraints where they conflict):

(a) The input is a BVA OPINION (often truncated to 18,000 chars), which has a strict structure: ORDER (one-line dispositions per issue) → FINDINGS OF FACT (numbered) → CONCLUSIONS OF LAW (numbered, each ending in a string of C.F.R./U.S.C. cites) → REASONS AND BASES (the main analytical body, with numbered subsections per issue). The REASONS AND BASES section is where almost all norm-bearing signals live. Aim for HIGH RECALL across the WHOLE Reasons-and-Bases section: 6-20 passages per opinion is typical (more for multi-issue opinions). The boilerplate AMA / Hearing-docket evidence-window paragraphs ("the Board may only consider the evidence of record at the time of the ... AOJ decision") emit at most ONE observation signal about the evidence-window rule — they are repeated verbatim across thousands of opinions and are not the action.

(b) ATTRIBUTION RULE — signals must capture THE BOARD'S OWN reasoning, not the parties' arguments quoted in the opinion. When the opinion says "The Veteran contends X", "The Veteran asserts Y", "Dr. Q.A. opined that ..." — the paraphrase of the veteran's argument, of a VA examiner, or of a private clinician is NOT itself a Board signal. The Board's signal is the Board's OWN move adopting, weighing, accepting, rejecting, or qualifying that evidence. The clearest cues are the Board's voice: "the Board finds", "the Board concludes", "the Board acknowledges", "the Board places greater weight on", "the Board affords low/significant/probative weight", "the Board recognizes", "the Board notes", "the evidence persuasively weighs against", "the benefit of the doubt doctrine [is/is not] for application", "warranted", "not warranted". Also acceptable: unattributed declarative statements of governing law ("Service connection requires competent evidence showing: (1) the existence of a present disability ...") which ARE the Board speaking in the doctrinal-exposition register. The Board's PROBATIVE-WEIGHT determinations on specific pieces of medical evidence (assigning probative value to a VA examiner's opinion, finding a private medical opinion conclusory, etc.) are paradigmatic norm signals.

(c) The Veteran's own LAY STATEMENTS are evidence to be weighed by the Board. When the Board cites a veteran's testimony for credibility analysis ("the Veteran's lay statements are competent and credible", "the Board acknowledges the Veteran's competent reports of experiencing depression since active service"), that is a Board signal evidencing the Layno / Jandreau / Buchanan competency-and-credibility norm. The lay statements themselves are not the signal.

(d) CITATION-INSIDE-PASSAGE: case citations integral to a reasoning move SHOULD be kept inside signal_text (e.g. "See Nieves-Rodriguez v. Peake, 22 Vet. App. 295 (2008)", "See Caluza v. Brown, 7 Vet. App. 498 (1995)", "Lynch v. McDonough, 21 F.4th 776 (Fed. Cir. 2021)"). C.F.R. and U.S.C. cites integral to a doctrinal exposition ("38 C.F.R. § 3.303(a)", "38 U.S.C. § 5107(b)") also belong inside signal_text when the Board is invoking that authority as the governing rule. signal_text 10-200 char window. A bare citation alone is NOT a signal.

(e) Bare procedural recitations — case caption, docket number, the Veteran's service dates, the rating decision being appealed, the date of the hearing or the AMA election, the AOJ history of the claim — emit ZERO signals unless the Board is using procedural posture to make a doctrinal move (e.g. invoking Fenderson because the appeal arose from the initial rating, invoking Rice v. Shinseki because TDIU was raised by the increased-rating claim, invoking Clemons v. Shinseki to broaden a psychiatric claim).

(f) PRESERVE the source text VERBATIM in passage_text and signal_text. BVA opinions contain PDF-conversion artifacts: section-symbol-as-question-mark ("38?C.F.R." instead of "38 C.F.R."), curly quotes, soft hyphens, en-dashes mid-word ("non?compensable"), tab characters between fields, line breaks mid-sentence in tabular hearing-test data. Copy character-for-character. Do not normalize, do not correct.

(g) When two or more discrete doctrinal moves appear in the same paragraph (e.g. the Board first states the Caluza elements, then applies them to the in-service-event prong), emit each as its own signal inside the same passage. 3-8 signals per substantive passage is typical.

(h) Multi-issue opinions: each numbered issue in the REASONS AND BASES section (e.g. "1. Entitlement to service connection for an acquired psychiatric disorder", "2. Entitlement to a disability rating in excess of 10 percent for ...") is its own analytical track. Aim to capture signals for EACH issue addressed in the truncated text, not only the first one.
